public_rationale: Support needs a court, regulator or company finding, or a specific Nadella statement from January 2023 to August 18, 2026 later shown false or materially incomplete about OpenAI's share. Contradiction needs records showing investors were fairly informed at the time, or a dismissal on the merits. Reuters reported on June 16, 2026 on a proposed shareholder class action over Azure growth and AI spending disclosures. Microsoft called the claims without merit (e1). AI Weekly, summarizing Bloomberg on August 5, 2026, reported $24.1 billion in OpenAI sales for the year ended June. Set against a $37 billion AI run rate it attributed to Nadella, it put OpenAI's implied share at more than half, possibly around 70% (e2). Benzinga reported on July 30, 2026 that CFO Amy Hood said commercial RPO grew 25% excluding OpenAI (e3). Silicon Lien wrote on August 3, 2026 that Microsoft had disclosed OpenAI was about 45% of December RPO (e4). Both concern backlog, not AI revenue. The cited items show no finding, no Nadella statement proven false, and no record that investors were fairly informed, so neither condition is met.
limitations: The evidence relies on news reports and secondary summaries. Microsoft's filings and earnings call transcripts were not read directly (HTTP 403).
The $24.1 billion figure comes from AI Weekly's summary of Bloomberg's report on a Microsoft filing. The filing itself was not read.
The 'more than half, possibly around 70%' figure is an implied ratio from AI Weekly's summary of Bloomberg. Microsoft did not disclose it, and Microsoft does not report an 'AI revenue' line.
Silicon Lien does not say when or how Microsoft disclosed the 45% backlog share (e4). Benzinga says Microsoft never disclosed OpenAI's backlog outright (e3). The two reports do not fully agree.

The statement in e3 is attributed to CFO Amy Hood, not Nadella. The disclosures in e3 and e4 concern backlog, not AI revenue. They do not show whether investors were fairly informed about OpenAI's share of AI revenue.
The quoted Reuters text does not name Nadella as a defendant. It does not show the case's current status or outcome.
The cited evidence includes no court, regulator or company finding on Microsoft's AI revenue disclosures. It does not show that no such finding exists.
The evidence identifies no specific Nadella statement about what drives Microsoft's AI revenue that can be checked against later disclosures.
Whether selective framing counts as 'misled' is partly a judgment, and readers may weigh it differently.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Satya Nadella has misled investors about how concentrated Microsoft's AI revenue is.

statement.excerpt: He’s the one that’s misled investors about the concentration of Microsoft’s AI revenue.

from_speaker: the concentration of Microsoft's AI revenue
our_interpretation: Plain reading: Satya Nadella made public statements to investors that gave a false or materially incomplete picture of how much of Microsoft's AI revenue came from a few customers, chiefly OpenAI.
The speaker gave no date. I read it as covering Nadella's investor communications from Microsoft's expanded OpenAI investment (January 2023) up to the post date (2026-08-18).

Because 'misled' is a charge of deception, a fair test needs an identifiable misleading statement. That could come from a court or regulator finding, a company correction or restatement, or a clear clash between a specific Nadella statement and later disclosed facts. Pending allegations or analyst ratios on their own do not settle it.
criteria.support_condition: A court or regulator finding, a settlement admission, a Microsoft correction, or a specific Nadella statement about AI revenue makeup that later disclosures clearly show was false or materially incomplete about OpenAI's share.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Records showing Microsoft and Nadella disclosed OpenAI's share of AI revenue or backlog at the time in a way that left investors fairly informed, or a court dismissing misleading-disclosure claims on the merits.

evidence.excerpt: Microsoft has been sued by shareholders who accused the company of defrauding them and inflating its stock price by failing to disclose slowing growth in its Azure cloud business
evidence.explanation: A pending class action naming Nadella alleges misleading disclosures. As reported, it focuses on Azure growth and AI spending, not on AI revenue concentration. Microsoft calls the claims without merit, and there is no finding.

evidence.excerpt: Set against Satya Nadella's earlier claim that the AI business was on a $37 billion annual run rate at the end of the March quarter, that implies OpenAI is driving more than half, and possibly around 70%
evidence.explanation: Shows that OpenAI's share of Microsoft's AI revenue was large: an implied ratio, not a disclosed figure. It does not show that any Nadella statement was false or misleading.

evidence.excerpt: The company never disclosed OpenAI‘s backlog outright. Instead, Hood told analysts that commercial RPO “increased 25% when excluding OpenAI.”
evidence.explanation: Microsoft gave investors OpenAI-excluded growth figures. That cuts against a charge of hiding concentration, though it was not a full breakdown.

evidence.excerpt: only Microsoft has disclosed a point-in-time share: OpenAI was about 45% of RPO in December
evidence.explanation: Microsoft told investors OpenAI's share of its backlog in January 2026. That counts against the claim that investors were kept in the dark about concentration.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A court ruling, settlement or SEC action that addresses Microsoft's AI revenue disclosures. Or a specific Nadella statement from January 2023 to August 18, 2026 about what drives Microsoft's AI revenue that Microsoft's later disclosures show was false or materially incomplete. Or Microsoft filings or call transcripts from that period showing that OpenAI's share of AI revenue was disclosed at the time in a way that left investors fairly informed.
